This sheet collects the key formulas of the course, organised by the chapters of
Collett (2023). Equation numbers in parentheses, e.g. (2.4), refer to the book's own
numbering; section references such as §2.2.1 point to where the formula is derived and
illustrated. Formulas that the book leaves unnumbered carry only a section reference.
Notation that recurs throughout is defined once below.

## Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $T$ | Survival (event) time of an individual |
| $C$ | Censoring time |
| $X = \min(T, C)$ | Observed follow-up time |
| $\delta = I(T \le C)$ | Event indicator ($1$ = event, $0$ = right-censored) |
| $F(t) = P(T \le t)$ | Distribution function of $T$ |
| $S(t) = P(T > t)$ | Survivor function |
| $f(t)$ | Probability density function of $T$ |
| $h(t)$ | Hazard function |
| $H(t)$ | Cumulative hazard function |
| $t_j$ | Ordered distinct event times ($j = 1, \dots, k$) |
| $n_j$ | Number at risk just before $t_j$ |
| $d_j$ | Number of events at $t_j$ |
| $c_j$ | Number censored in the interval ending at $t_j$ |
| $\mathcal{R}(t)$ | Risk set at $t$: individuals still at risk just before $t$ |
| $\mathbf{x}_i$ | Vector of covariates for individual $i$ |
| $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ | Vector of regression coefficients |
| $\eta_i = \boldsymbol{\beta}'\mathbf{x}_i$ | Linear predictor (risk score / prognostic index) |
| $\psi = \exp(\beta)$ | Hazard ratio |

## 1. Survival analysis

*Fundamentals, censoring, and the three key functions* (§1.2, §1.4).

Distribution function (1.1):

$$F(t) = P(T \le t) = \int_0^t f(u)\,\mathrm{d}u. \qquad (1.1)$$

Survivor function (1.2):

$$S(t) = P(T > t) = 1 - F(t). \qquad (1.2)$$

Density (from the definitions in §1.4.1):

$$f(t) = \frac{\mathrm{d}F(t)}{\mathrm{d}t} = -S'(t).$$

Hazard function — the instantaneous event rate among those still at risk (1.3), equal to
the density divided by the survivor function (1.4):

$$h(t) = \lim_{\delta \to 0} \frac{P(t \le T < t + \delta \mid T \ge t)}{\delta} \qquad (1.3)
\qquad h(t) = \frac{f(t)}{S(t)}. \qquad (1.4)$$

Relations linking the three functions (1.5)–(1.8):

$$h(t) = -\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\log S(t), \qquad (1.5)$$
$$S(t) = \exp\{-H(t)\}, \qquad (1.6)$$
$$H(t) = \int_0^t h(u)\,\mathrm{d}u, \qquad (1.7)$$
$$H(t) = -\log S(t). \qquad (1.8)$$

Also $f(t) = h(t)\,S(t)$, which follows from (1.4).

Right-censoring: we observe $X = \min(T, C)$ and $\delta = I(T \le C)$. Under
*independent censoring*, the censoring mechanism carries no information about $T$ beyond
the censoring time (§1.2.2).

## 2. Some non-parametric procedures

*Kaplan–Meier, Nelson–Aalen, the life table, standard errors, and group comparisons*
(§2.1–2.9).

Kaplan–Meier (product-limit) estimate of the survivor function (2.4):

$$\hat S(t) = \prod_{t_j \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_j}{n_j}\right) = \prod_{t_j \le t} \frac{n_j - d_j}{n_j}. \qquad (2.4)$$

Nelson–Aalen estimate of the cumulative hazard, and the survivor estimate derived from
it (2.5):

$$\tilde H(t) = \sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_j}{n_j}, \qquad \tilde S(t) = \exp\{-\tilde H(t)\} = \prod_{t_j \le t} \exp(-d_j/n_j). \qquad (2.5)$$

Life-table estimate uses the effective number at risk (2.2) in the product (2.3):

$$n'_j = n_j - c_j/2 \qquad (2.2) \qquad
\hat S(t) = \prod_{j} \left(1 - \frac{d_j}{n'_j}\right). \qquad (2.3)$$

Greenwood's formula — estimated variance (2.11) and standard error (2.12) of $\hat S(t)$:

$$\operatorname{var}\{\hat S(t)\} = \hat S(t)^2 \sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_j}{n_j(n_j - d_j)}, \qquad (2.11)$$
$$\operatorname{se}\{\hat S(t)\} = \hat S(t) \sqrt{\sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_j}{n_j(n_j - d_j)}}. \qquad (2.12)$$

Confidence intervals: the plain Wald interval $\hat S \pm 1.96\,\operatorname{se}$ can
leave $[0,1]$; a log or log-log transformation is preferred in practice (§2.2.3).

Estimated median survival time: the smallest $t$ for which $\hat S(t) < 0.5$ (§2.4).

Log-rank test for two groups (§2.6.2). With $e_{1j} = n_{1j} d_j / n_j$ the expected
events in group 1 under the null (2.19),

$$e_{1j} = n_{1j} d_j / n_j, \qquad (2.19)$$
$$U_L = \sum_{j} (d_{1j} - e_{1j}), \qquad (2.20)$$
$$v_{1j} = \frac{n_{1j} n_{2j} d_j (n_j - d_j)}{n_j^2 (n_j - 1)}, \qquad (2.21)$$
$$V_L = \sum_j v_{1j}, \qquad \frac{U_L^2}{V_L} \sim \chi^2_1. \qquad (2.23)$$

The Wilcoxon test weights each contribution by $n_j$ (more sensitive to early
differences); the Peto–Peto test weights by an estimate of $S(t)$ (preferred when
censoring patterns differ) (§2.6.3–2.6.5). Stratified tests combine the $U$ and $V$
contributions over strata (2.25); the log-rank test for trend uses weighted sums over
ordered categories (2.26)–(2.27) (§2.8–2.9).

## 3. The Cox regression model

*The proportional hazards model, partial likelihood, and inference* (§3.1–3.14).

Model for the hazard of individual $i$ (general form, 3.3):

$$h_i(t) = h_0(t)\exp(\boldsymbol{\beta}'\mathbf{x}_i) = h_0(t)\exp(\eta_i). \qquad (3.3)$$

The baseline hazard $h_0(t)$ is left unspecified (semi-parametric). For two treatment
groups (3.1) gives $h_N(t) = \psi\, h_S(t)$, i.e. a constant hazard ratio
$\psi = \exp(\beta)$.

Partial likelihood (no ties); the product runs over event times with risk sets
$\mathcal{R}(t_i)$ (3.5), with log-likelihood (3.6):

$$L(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \prod_{i : \delta_i = 1} \frac{\exp(\eta_i)}{\sum_{\ell \in \mathcal{R}(t_i)} \exp(\eta_\ell)}, \qquad (3.5)$$
$$\log L(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \sum_{i : \delta_i = 1} \left\{ \eta_i - \log \sum_{\ell \in \mathcal{R}(t_i)} \exp(\eta_\ell) \right\}. \qquad (3.6)$$

Estimation maximises $\log L$ (Newton–Raphson using the score $U$ and information
$I$); $\operatorname{se}(\hat\beta_j) = (I^{-1})_{jj}^{1/2}$ (§3.3.3).

Hazard ratio and its confidence interval (§3.4, §3.4.1): a $100(1-\alpha)\%$ interval for
$\beta$ is

$$\hat\beta \pm z_{\alpha/2}\,\operatorname{se}(\hat\beta),$$

then exponentiate to obtain the interval for $\psi$. The standard error of $\hat\psi$
follows from (3.13):

$$\operatorname{se}(\hat\psi) = \hat\psi\,\operatorname{se}(\hat\beta). \qquad (3.13)$$

Model comparison (§3.5): the statistic $-2\log \hat L$ is compared between nested models,

$$\Delta(-2\log \hat L) \sim \chi^2_{p - q},$$

where $p - q$ is the difference in the number of parameters. Akaike's information
criterion (3.14):

$$\mathrm{AIC} = -2\log \hat L + 2q. \qquad (3.14)$$

Estimated survivor function for a given covariate pattern (§3.10, 3.26):

$$\hat S_i(t) = \{\hat S_0(t)\}^{\exp(\hat\eta_i)}. \qquad (3.26)$$

With no covariates this reduces to the Kaplan–Meier estimate (§3.10.1).

Further tools: the lasso adds the penalty $\lambda \sum_j |\beta_j|$ to the partial
log-likelihood (3.16); fractional polynomials model non-linearity (§3.8); the
concordance $c$-index and $R^2$-type measures assess predictive ability (§3.12);
time-dependent ROC curves assess discrimination over time (§3.13). The Cox score test is
identical to the log-rank test when there is a single binary covariate (§3.14).

## 4. Model checking in the Cox regression model

*Residuals and the proportional hazards assumption* (§4.1–4.5).

Cox–Snell residuals (4.1):

$$r_{Ci} = \hat H_0(t_i)\exp(\hat\eta_i) = -\log \hat S_i(t_i). \qquad (4.1)$$

Martingale residuals (4.6):

$$r_{Mi} = \delta_i - r_{Ci}. \qquad (4.6)$$

Deviance residuals (4.7):

$$r_{Di} = \operatorname{sign}(r_{Mi})\sqrt{-2\left[r_{Mi} + \delta_i\log(\delta_i - r_{Mi})\right]}. \qquad (4.7)$$

Schoenfeld residuals for covariate $j$ at each event time (4.8):

$$r_{Sji} = \delta_i\{x_{ji} - \hat a_{ji}\}. \qquad (4.8)$$

Score residuals (4.13) are the building blocks of influence diagnostics (§4.3). The
proportional hazards assumption is tested from the Schoenfeld residuals: under PH,
$E(r_{Sji}) \approx \beta_j(t_i) - \hat\beta_j$ (4.18), so a systematic trend against time
leads to the test statistic (4.19)–(4.20) (§4.4.2–4.4.3). Adding a time-dependent
variable (4.22) is the regression-based alternative (§4.4.4).

## 5. Parametric regression models

*Fully parametric hazard and accelerated failure time models* (§5.1–5.17).

Common distributions (hazard $h(t)$, survivor $S(t)$):

| Distribution | $h(t)$ | $S(t)$ |
|---|---|---|
| Exponential | $\lambda$ (5.2) | $\exp(-\lambda t)$ (5.2) |
| Weibull | $\lambda\gamma t^{\gamma-1}$ (5.4) | $\exp(-\lambda t^{\gamma})$ (5.5) |
| Log-logistic | $\dfrac{\lambda\gamma(\lambda t)^{\gamma-1}}{1 + (\lambda t)^{\gamma}}$ (5.8) | $\dfrac{1}{1 + (\lambda t)^{\gamma}}$ (5.9) |
| Lognormal | — (§5.1.4) | $1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{\log t - \mu}{\sigma}\right)$ (5.10) |
| Gompertz | $\lambda \exp(\theta t)$ (§5.1.5) | $\exp\{-\frac{\lambda}{\theta}(e^{\theta t} - 1)\}$ (§5.1.5) |

Here $\lambda > 0$ is a scale and $\gamma > 0$ a shape parameter ($\gamma = 1$ recovers
the exponential); gamma and inverse Gaussian are further options (§5.1.6–5.1.8). A
Weibull diagnostic plot uses (5.12):

$$\log\{-\log S(t)\} = \log\lambda + \gamma\log t. \qquad (5.12)$$

Weibull proportional hazards model (5.42)–(5.43):

$$h_i(t) = \gamma t^{\gamma-1}\exp(\boldsymbol{\beta}'\mathbf{x}_i), \qquad (5.42)$$
$$S_i(t) = \exp\{-\exp(\boldsymbol{\beta}'\mathbf{x}_i)\,\lambda t^{\gamma}\}. \qquad (5.43)$$

Accelerated failure time (AFT) models (§5.10–5.12). General hazard form (5.60) and
log-linear form (5.61):

$$h_i(t) = e^{-\eta_i}\,h_0(t/e^{\eta_i}), \qquad (5.60)$$
$$\log T_i = \mu + \boldsymbol{\beta}'\mathbf{x}_i + \sigma W_i, \qquad (5.61)$$

where $W$ has a standard distribution. The Weibull is the only distribution that is
simultaneously PH and AFT.

Proportional odds model (5.76):

$$\frac{S_i(t)}{1 - S_i(t)} = e^{\eta_i}\frac{S_0(t)}{1 - S_0(t)}. \qquad (5.76)$$

Cure-rate model (5.79):

$$S(t) = (1 - \pi)S_n(t) + \pi. \qquad (5.79)$$

## 6. Flexible parametric models

*Piecewise and spline-based models* (§6.1–6.5).

Piecewise exponential model: constant hazard within each interval (6.1),

$$h_0(t) = \lambda_j \quad \text{on interval } j. \qquad (6.1)$$

Restricted cubic spline (RCS) in $t$ (6.7)–(6.8):

$$s(t) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 t + \sum_{j} \gamma_{j+1}\nu_j(t), \qquad (6.7)$$
$$\nu_j(t) = (t - k_j)_+^3 - \lambda_j(t - k_{\min})_+^3 - (1 - \lambda_j)(t - k_{\max})_+^3. \qquad (6.8)$$

Royston–Parmar model: the log cumulative hazard is an RCS in $y = \log t$ (6.13):

$$\log H_i(t) = \eta_i + \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 y + \sum_j \gamma_{j+1}\nu_j(y). \qquad (6.13)$$

## 7. Model checking in parametric models

*Residuals and diagnostics for parametric models* (§7.1–7.5).

Standardised residuals (7.1):

$$r_{Si} = \frac{\log t_i - \hat\mu - \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}'\mathbf{x}_i}{\hat\sigma}. \qquad (7.1)$$

Cox–Snell (7.2), martingale (7.4) and deviance (7.5) residuals carry over, now based on
the fitted parametric $S(t)$ and $H(t)$:

$$r_{Ci} = \hat H_i(t_i) = -\log \hat S_i(t_i), \qquad (7.2)$$
$$r_{Mi} = \delta_i - r_{Ci}, \qquad (7.4)$$
$$r_{Di} = \operatorname{sign}(r_{Mi})\sqrt{-2\left[r_{Mi} + \delta_i\log(\delta_i - r_{Mi})\right]}. \qquad (7.5)$$

Fitted and observed survivor functions are compared visually (§7.3), and influential
observations are identified from the score residuals (§7.4).

## 8. Time-dependent variables

*Covariates and coefficients that change over time* (§8.1–8.7).

Time-dependent covariate $x(t)$ (8.1), with survivor function (8.4):

$$h_i(t) = h_0(t)\exp\{\boldsymbol{\beta}'\mathbf{x}_i(t)\}, \qquad (8.1)$$
$$S_i(t) = \exp\left[-\int_0^t \exp\{\boldsymbol{\beta}'\mathbf{x}_i(u)\}\,h_0(u)\,\mathrm{d}u\right]. \qquad (8.4)$$

Time-varying coefficient $\beta(t)$ allows a covariate's effect to change over time
(§8.1.1). Joint models couple a longitudinal submodel for repeated measurements with a
survival submodel (8.10):

$$h_i(t) = \exp\{\boldsymbol{\beta}'\mathbf{x}_i + \alpha\, m_i(t)\}\,h_0(t). \qquad (8.10)$$

## 9. Interval-censored survival data

*When the event time is known only up to an interval* (§9.1–9.4).

The non-parametric maximum likelihood estimate (Turnbull) of $S(t)$ puts mass
$\hat\theta_j$ on the Turnbull intervals $(a_j, b_j]$ and is (9.2):

$$\hat S(t) = \prod_{t_j \le t} \hat\theta_j. \qquad (9.2)$$

The likelihood for interval-censored data is (9.3):

$$L = \prod_i \{S(l_i) - S(u_i)\}. \qquad (9.3)$$

Semi-parametric (piecewise exponential) and parametric alternatives are described in
§9.3–9.4.

## 10. Frailty models

*Unobserved heterogeneity and clustered data* (§10.1–10.8).

Individual frailty $Z_i$ scales the hazard (10.2):

$$h_i(t \mid Z_i) = Z_i\, h_0(t)\exp(\boldsymbol{\beta}'\mathbf{x}_i). \qquad (10.2)$$

With gamma frailty $Z_i \sim \operatorname{Gamma}(1/\theta,\,1/\theta)$ (mean 1, variance
$\theta$), the observable survivor function is (10.12):

$$S_i^*(t) = \{1 + \theta^{-1}e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}'\mathbf{x}_i}H_0(t)\}^{-\theta}. \qquad (10.12)$$

The shared frailty model assigns a common $Z_i$ to all members of a cluster (10.31):

$$h_{ij}(t \mid Z_i) = Z_i\, h_0(t)\exp(\boldsymbol{\beta}'\mathbf{x}_{ij}). \qquad (10.31)$$

## 11. Non-proportional hazards and institutional comparisons

*Stratification, restricted mean survival, and random effects* (§11.1–11.4).

Stratified proportional hazards model — separate baseline hazard per stratum, common
coefficients (§11.2):

$$h_{sk}(t) = h_{0k}(t)\exp(\boldsymbol{\beta}'\mathbf{x}).$$

Restricted mean survival time over $[0, t_0]$ (§11.3):

$$\mu(t_0) = E\{\min(T, t_0)\} = \int_0^{t_0} S(u)\,\mathrm{d}u.$$

The pseudo-value for individual $i$ is (11.4):

$$z_i = n\,\hat\mu(t_0) - (n-1)\,\hat\mu_{(-i)}(t_0). \qquad (11.4)$$

Institutional comparisons use random-effect (frailty) or Poisson formulations, comparing
observed to expected failures via (11.8) (§11.4).

## 12. Competing risks

*Cause-specific hazards and the cumulative incidence function* (§12.1–12.6).

Cause-specific hazard for cause $j$ (12.1):

$$\lambda_j(t) = \lim_{\delta \to 0} \frac{P(t \le T < t + \delta, K = j \mid T \ge t)}{\delta}. \qquad (12.1)$$

Cumulative incidence function — the probability of an event *of cause* $j$ by time $t$
(12.4):

$$F_j(t) = \int_0^t \lambda_j(u)\, S(u)\,\mathrm{d}u, \qquad (12.4)$$

estimated by (12.5):

$$\hat F_j(t) = \sum_{t_i \le t} \frac{\delta_{ij}}{n_i}\,\hat S(t_{i-1}). \qquad (12.5)$$

Fine–Gray subdistribution hazard (12.10) and its proportional model (12.11):

$$\gamma_j(t) = -\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\log\{1 - F_j(t)\}, \qquad (12.10)$$
$$\lambda_{ij}(t) = \exp(\boldsymbol{\beta}_j'\mathbf{x}_i)\,\lambda_{0j}(t). \qquad (12.11)$$

Note that $1 - \sum_j F_j(t) = S(t)$; the cumulative incidence of one cause depends on
the hazards of all causes.

## 13. Multiple events and event history modelling

*Counting processes and recurrent events* (§13.1–13.5).

A counting process $N_i(t)$ counts events up to $t$; its intensity is (13.1), which for
survival data reduces to the at-risk indicator times the hazard (13.4):

$$\lambda_i(t)\,\mathrm{d}t = Y_i(t)\,h_i(t)\,\mathrm{d}t. \qquad (13.4)$$

The martingale is $M_i(t) = N_i(t) - \Lambda_i(t)$ (13.3). Models for recurrent events:
Anderson–Gill (13.5) and Prentice–Williams–Peterson (13.6):

$$h_i(t) = Y_i(t)\exp\{\boldsymbol{\beta}'\mathbf{x}_i(t)\}\,h_0(t), \qquad (13.5)$$
$$h_{ij}(t) = Y_{ij}(t)\exp\{\boldsymbol{\beta}_j'\mathbf{x}_i(t)\}\,h_{0j}(t). \qquad (13.6)$$

Wei–Lin–Weissfeld uses marginal models per event (§13.3). Robust (sandwich) standard
errors accommodate within-subject correlation (§13.1.4).

## 14. Dependent censoring

*When censoring is informative* (§14.1–14.3).

Inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW) reweights individuals by the inverse of
the estimated probability of remaining uncensored, obtained from a censoring model (14.3),
entering the weighted partial likelihood (14.4):

$$\hat S_{ci}(t) = \{\hat S_{c0}(t)\}^{\exp(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_c'\mathbf{x}_i)}. \qquad (14.3)$$

## 15. Sample size requirements for a survival study

*Number of events and number of patients* (§15.1–15.3).

Required number of events (deaths) to detect a hazard ratio $\psi$ with two-sided level
$\alpha$ and power $1-\beta$, allocation proportions $\pi_1, \pi_2$ (15.1); equal
allocation gives (15.2):

$$d = \frac{(z_{\alpha/2} + z_{\beta})^2}{\pi_1 \pi_2 \,(\log \psi)^2}, \qquad (15.1)$$
$$d = \frac{4(z_{\alpha/2} + z_{\beta})^2}{(\log \psi)^2}. \qquad (15.2)$$

The required number of patients follows by inflating for the probability of an event by
the end of follow-up (15.10):

$$n = \frac{d}{P(\text{event})}, \qquad (15.10)$$

where $P(\text{event})$ is obtained from the survivor function, e.g. via Simpson's rule
(15.11) (§15.3).

## 16. Bayesian survival analysis

*Priors, posteriors, and model comparison* (§16.1–16.10).

Bayes' theorem for the model parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ (16.4):

$$p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \text{data}) = \frac{L(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\int L(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}}. \qquad (16.4)$$

The likelihood for survival data is (16.5):

$$L(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid t) = \prod_i \{h_i(t_i)\}^{\delta_i}\,S_i(t_i). \qquad (16.5)$$

Model comparison uses the deviance information criterion (16.15) and the widely
applicable information criterion (16.16):

$$\mathrm{DIC} = D(\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) + 2p_D, \qquad (16.15)$$
$$\mathrm{WAIC} = -2\sum_i \log p(t_i \mid t) + 2p_W. \qquad (16.16)$$

## 17. Survival analysis with R

*Mapping the methods to the `survival` package* (§17.1–17.16).

| Task | Function |
|---|---|
| Create a survival object | `Surv(time, event)` |
| Kaplan–Meier / Nelson–Aalen curves | `survfit()` |
| Log-rank and related tests | `survdiff()` |
| Cox regression | `coxph()` |
| PH diagnostics and residuals | `cox.zph()`, `residuals(..., type = "...")` |
| Parametric models (PH and AFT) | `survreg()` |
| Flexible (Royston–Parmar) models | `flexsurv::flexsurvspline()` |
| Competing risks (Fine–Gray) | `cmprsk::crr()` / `tidycmprsk` |
| Kaplan–Meier plots | `ggsurvfit::ggsurvfit()` |

The parametric log-linear form (17.1) and the frailty model (17.2) restate (5.61) and
(10.2) in the notation used by `survreg` and `coxph`:

$$\log T_i = \mu + \boldsymbol{\alpha}'\mathbf{x}_i + \sigma\varepsilon_i, \qquad (17.1)$$
$$h_i(t) = z_i\exp(\boldsymbol{\beta}'\mathbf{x}_i)\,h_0(t). \qquad (17.2)$$

## Appendices

Appendix A summarises maximum likelihood estimation for one and several parameters
(score, information, standard errors) — the machinery behind the estimators above.
Appendix B lists five additional data sets (chronic active hepatitis, bladder cancer,
black ducks, bone marrow transplantation, chronic granulomatous disease) that can be
used for practice analyses.
